blocks.text: [II, 473] Now, that the animal which the Arabs have described to us under the names ضب [ḍabb] dhab and حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun is the very same as the צב tsab of Moses is shown by so many arguments that it would be wrong to doubt [II, 474] it. First, it is supported by the similarity of the Hebrew name to the Arabic. For however much the Hebrew צב tsab and the Arabic ضب [ḍabb] dhab differ in sound, in both the initial letter is Tsade, which the Arabs pronounce differently because of the added point. Nothing is more frequent than this change. Thus צאן tson, sheep, in Hebrew, is ضان [ḍān] dhan in Arabic. Hyena is צבוע tsebua in the one, ضبع [ḍabuʿ] dhebu in the other. Frog is צפרדע tsephardea in the one, ضفدع [ḍifdaʿ] dhephda in the other. Rib is צלע tsela in the one, ضلع [ḍilʿ] dhila in the other. Diadem, or braid of hair, is צפירה tsephira in the one, ضفيرة [ḍafīra] [col. 1054] dhephira in the other. Dung is צפיע tsephia in the one, ضفع [ḍfʿ] dhepha in the other. Narrowness is צרק tsuk in the one, ضيق [ḍīq] dhik in the other. To laugh is צחק tsachak in the one, ضحق [ḍḥq] dhachika in the other. 2. Second, that צב tsab is what we have said is made plain by the series of related animals in the same context. For in the following verse mention is made of the lizard, the stellio, the chameleon, the salamander, etc., as will be shown in its place. And there was equal reason for this species of lizard to be rejected as unclean. Nor could it be omitted, since it is native to Arabia, which borders on Judaea, and is eaten among the Arabs. 3. To this is added the authority of the ancients, of whom I affirm there is none who took it otherwise. Certainly the four Arabic versions I have been able to consult, two printed and two manuscript [II, 475], although they differ much from one another elsewhere, here consistently have الضب [al-ḍabb] aldhab; and Onkelos has צבא tsaba, which is the very Hebrew word, with only the ending adapted to Chaldee. In Jonathan you read חרדונא chardona for צב tsab; in the Syriac ܚܕܪܘܢܐ chadrona; and in the Samaritan [?] adrona: these three come to the same thing. What is meant, namely, is the Arabs' حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun, which Avicenna asserted above ^{c)} to be the same as ضب [ḍabb] dhab. Some hold that it is similar to it, others that it is its male. Damir: الحردون دويبة شبيه بالضب وقيل هو ذكر الضب لان له ذكرين مثله [al-ḥardūn duwaybba shabīh bi-l-ḍabb wa-qīla huwa dhakar al-ḍabb li-anna lahu dhakarayn mithlahu] Alchardaun (or rather alchirdaun, for he directs it to be written so) is a small animal similar to τῷ [tō] dhab: indeed it is said to be its male, because like it it has two penises. Alcamus: الحردون لذكر الضب ودويبة احري [al-ḥardūn li-dhakar al-ḍabb wa-duwaybba aḥrī] Alchardaun (is said) of the male τοῦ [tou] dhab. It is also another (similar) small animal ^{(2)}.
